title: Reproductive Biochemistry and Nutrition
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: Reproduction runs on specific nutrients and fuels, and this chapter follows each one to its mechanism. It covers folate in DNA synthesis and neural tube closure, the iron cost of pregnancy, lactose and immune proteins in milk, glucose transfer across the placenta, zinc and vitamin A in sexual and embryonic development, the energy signal that permits GnRH pulsatility, and the cholesterol supply for sex steroids. Board questions typically describe a deficiency, an excess, or a lab pattern in a mother, fetus, newborn, or athlete and ask you to predict the consequence or name the step involved. Each answer follows from knowing what the nutrient does at the molecular level and when in development it is needed.

connections.how: The same folate and iron mechanisms that affect pregnancy explain megaloblastic and microcytic anemias in any patient.
Folate and retinoic acid act on neurulation and neural crest patterning, which explains the timing and type of birth defects.
Placental hormones create maternal insulin resistance, and fetal insulin drives the growth seen in diabetic pregnancy.
Secretory IgA in milk is the classic example of passive mucosal immunity transferred from mother to infant.
Estrogen loss in hypothalamic amenorrhea raises osteoclast activity and lowers bone density.

sections.title: Folate in thymidylate and purine synthesis, and neural tube defects

blocks.text: Folate is a water-soluble B vitamin; folic acid is its synthetic, oxidized form. To work, it must be reduced by dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), using NADPH, to tetrahydrofolate (THF). THF carries single carbon units at different oxidation levels (methyl, methylene, formyl), and the cell spends these units on two DNA building blocks: thymidylate and the purine ring. Body folate stores last only a few months, so intake must be continuous.

Thymidylate synthase transfers a methylene group from 5,10-methylene-THF to dUMP and then reduces it to a methyl group, forming dTMP. The reducing power comes from the folate itself, so the reaction leaves dihydrofolate (DHF), which must be reduced again by DHFR before it can carry another carbon. This makes thymidylate synthesis the step most sensitive to folate supply and explains why DHFR inhibitors (methotrexate in human cells, trimethoprim in bacteria) stop DNA synthesis even when folate is present. In de novo purine synthesis, two transformylase steps take carbons from 10-formyl-THF to build carbons 2 and 8 of the ring on the way to IMP.

blocks.title: The thymidylate folate cycle
steps: THF picks up a carbon from serine
5,10-methylene-THF donates it to dUMP
dTMP forms; folate is oxidized to DHF
DHFR and NADPH reduce DHF back to THF
blocks.caption: Each dTMP made costs one reduction by DHFR, so blocking DHFR or lacking folate halts thymidylate supply.

blocks.text: Folate also links to vitamin B12. Methionine synthase uses B12 to move the methyl group from 5-methyl-THF to homocysteine, making methionine and freeing THF. Without B12, folate is trapped as 5-methyl-THF (the methyl trap), so both deficiencies impair DNA synthesis and raise homocysteine, but only B12 deficiency raises methylmalonic acid.

When dTMP runs short, the dUTP to dTTP ratio rises and DNA polymerase inserts uracil. Repair enzymes excise it repeatedly but cannot fill the gaps without dTTP, so strands break and cells stall in S phase or die. Rapidly dividing tissues suffer first: marrow (megaloblastic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils) and, in the embryo, the neuroepithelium.

In week 3 the notochord induces ectoderm to form the neural plate. Its folds rise and fuse first near the future cervical region at about day 22, then zip toward both ends. The cranial neuropore closes at about day 25 and the caudal neuropore at about day 27 to 28, often before a pregnancy is recognized, so folate status at conception is what matters. Failure of cranial closure causes anencephaly, and failure of caudal closure causes spina bifida with meningocele or myelomeningocele. Open defects leak alpha-fetoprotein into amniotic fluid and maternal serum, and amniotic acetylcholinesterase confirms an open lesion. Neural tube defects are multifactorial: folate deficiency, reduced-activity MTHFR variants, folate-antagonist or certain antiepileptic drugs (valproate), maternal pregestational diabetes, and obesity all raise risk.

blocks.title: Folate forms and what they supply
rows: Methylene (reduced to methyl in the reaction)
Carbons 2 and 8 of the purine ring
blocks.caption: Shortage of any form slows DNA synthesis; the thymidylate step fails first.

blocks.predict: A patient on methotrexate takes high-dose folic acid supplements. Will thymidylate synthesis recover?
blocks.explain: No. Folic acid is the oxidized form and needs DHFR to become THF, and thymidylate synthase turns THF into DHF with every dTMP it makes. With DHFR blocked, neither supplement nor recycled folate can be reduced, so the folate pool collapses into DHF.

sections.title: Iron requirement of pregnancy and dilutional versus iron deficiency anemia

blocks.text: Pregnancy needs about 1 g of iron beyond ordinary needs, most of it in the second half. The maternal red cell mass expands, the fetus and placenta build their own iron stores and hemoglobin, and basal losses continue. Dietary iron rarely covers this, so the mother draws on her stores, and many women begin pregnancy with low ones.

blocks.title: Approximate iron cost of a singleton pregnancy
rows: Expansion of maternal red cell mass
blocks.caption: Part of the red cell iron returns to stores after delivery, but blood lost at delivery is not recovered.

blocks.text: The body adapts by raising absorption. Hepcidin, the liver hormone that degrades the iron exporter ferroportin, falls in the second and third trimesters, so enterocytes release more iron into plasma. The placenta takes up maternal transferrin through transferrin receptors on the syncytiotrophoblast and exports iron to fetal transferrin. Transfer runs one way and favors the fetus, so the newborn is rarely anemic, but severe maternal deficiency still reduces fetal iron stores.

Plasma volume rises by about 40 to 50% because renin, angiotensin, and aldosterone activity increase and sodium and water are retained, while red cell mass rises by only about 20 to 30% under erythropoietin. Hemoglobin concentration therefore falls by dilution, most noticeably in the second trimester, even when iron is adequate. Lower viscosity eases placental perfusion, so this physiologic anemia is an adaptation, not a disease.

True iron deficiency follows a fixed sequence. Ferritin, which reflects storage iron, falls first. Serum iron and transferrin saturation then fall, and hemoglobin synthesis becomes iron-limited, so new cells come out small and pale, the MCV drops, and the RDW widens as microcytes mix with older normal cells. Two pregnancy effects complicate the labs. Estrogen raises hepatic transferrin synthesis, so TIBC rises in every pregnancy and cannot diagnose deficiency on its own, and MCV normally rises a few femtoliters, so a normal MCV can hide early deficiency. Ferritin is therefore the deciding test, read with care because inflammation raises it as an acute phase reactant.

blocks.title: Physiologic dilution versus iron deficiency in pregnancy
rows: Mildly low, rarely below about 10.5 g/dL
Low (below about 30 ng/mL), the earliest change
Plasma volume outpaces red cell mass

blocks.caption: Ferritin separates the two; TIBC rises in both, and MCV changes late.

blocks.title: Reading pregnancy iron studies
blocks.text: At 26 weeks, hemoglobin is 10.4 g/dL, MCV 88 fL, ferritin 9 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 10%, and TIBC high. The normal MCV first suggests dilution, but ferritin of 9 ng/mL means stores are empty. MCV has not yet fallen because microcytes are only beginning to enter a circulation of older normocytic cells, and the normal pregnancy rise in MCV masks the change. The high TIBC adds nothing, since estrogen raises it in all pregnancies. The diagnosis is early iron deficiency. If ferritin had been 60 ng/mL with the same hemoglobin and MCV, the picture would fit dilution. A low MCV with normal ferritin would point instead to another cause, such as thalassemia trait.

sections.title: Lactose synthesis and the composition of human milk

blocks.text: Lactose (galactose beta-1,4 glucose) is made in the Golgi lumen of mammary alveolar cells. Glucose enters the cell through GLUT1, and part of it is converted to UDP-glucose and then, by UDP-galactose 4-epimerase, to UDP-galactose, so the gland needs no dietary galactose. Both substrates move into the Golgi.

Lactose synthase has two subunits. The catalytic one, beta-1,4-galactosyltransferase, normally adds galactose to N-acetylglucosamine on glycoproteins and has very low affinity for free glucose. The regulatory subunit, alpha-lactalbumin, binds the enzyme and lowers its Km for glucose roughly a thousandfold, so the complex joins UDP-galactose to glucose to make lactose. Alpha-lactalbumin is made only in the lactating gland. Prolactin induces it, and high progesterone suppresses it during pregnancy, so copious milk production (lactogenesis II) begins only when progesterone falls after delivery of the placenta.

Lactose cannot cross the Golgi or secretory vesicle membranes, so it holds water osmotically inside the vesicles. Lactose is therefore the main osmole of milk and sets its volume, so milk stays isosmotic with plasma and lactose concentration changes little as volume rises or falls.

blocks.title: Mature human milk compared with cow milk (approximate, per dL)
blocks.caption: Human milk is high in lactose and low in protein, with a whey-dominant protein mix that is easy to digest.

blocks.text: Colostrum, made in the first days, is richer in protein and secretory IgA and lower in lactose. Secretory IgA comes from plasma cells in the breast that originated in maternal gut-associated lymphoid tissue (the enteromammary pathway), so it targets microbes the mother has met. The polymeric immunoglobulin receptor carries dimeric IgA across the epithelium, and the retained secretory component protects it from proteolysis in the infant gut. There it blocks microbial adherence without activating complement or inflammation. Lactoferrin binds the iron that bacteria need, and lysozyme hydrolyzes bacterial peptidoglycan.

Milk is poor in two fat-soluble vitamins. Low vitamin D leaves an infant with little sun exposure at risk of rickets. Vitamin K is low in milk, crosses the placenta poorly, and is not yet supplied by gut bacteria, so the newborn has little to gamma-carboxylate factors II, VII, IX, and X and proteins C and S. The result is vitamin K deficiency bleeding, with a prolonged PT and normal platelet count.

sections.title: Placental glucose transfer and the fetus of a hyperglycemic mother

blocks.text: Glucose is the main fuel of the fetus, which makes little of its own. It crosses the syncytiotrophoblast by facilitated diffusion through GLUT1 on both the maternal-facing microvillous membrane and the fetal-facing basal membrane. The process is carrier-mediated and saturable but needs no energy, so the flux depends on the concentration gradient, and fetal glucose runs at about 70 to 80% of maternal glucose. Maternal insulin, a peptide hormone with no transport route across the placenta, stays on the maternal side.

As pregnancy advances, human placental lactogen, placental growth hormone, progesterone, and cortisol make the mother progressively insulin resistant. This diverts glucose toward the fetus. A mother whose beta cells cannot raise insulin output enough becomes hyperglycemic (gestational diabetes), and pregestational diabetes produces the same fetal exposure.

blocks.title: Maternal hyperglycemia to neonatal hypoglycemia
steps: Maternal glucose rises; maternal insulin cannot cross
Glucose crosses by GLUT1; fetal glucose rises
Fetal beta cells hypertrophy and oversecrete insulin
Fetal insulin drives fat, glycogen, and organ growth
Cord clamped: glucose supply stops, insulin stays high
Neonatal hypoglycemia in the first hours
blocks.caption: Glucose crosses and insulin does not, so the fetus answers maternal hyperglycemia with its own insulin.

blocks.text: Fetal insulin acts as a growth hormone. It promotes fat deposition, hepatic glycogen, and growth of insulin-sensitive organs, producing macrosomia with hepatomegaly and cardiomegaly that can include interventricular septal hypertrophy. The brain is not insulin dependent, so the head grows normally while the shoulders and trunk enlarge, which explains the risk of shoulder dystocia. Hyperinsulinemia raises fetal metabolic rate and oxygen consumption, and the relative hypoxemia stimulates erythropoietin, causing polycythemia and later hyperbilirubinemia. Insulin also antagonizes cortisol's induction of surfactant synthesis in type II pneumocytes, so respiratory distress is more likely at a given gestational age.

At birth the maternal glucose supply ends abruptly, but the hyperplastic beta cells keep secreting insulin, which suppresses glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, so glucose falls within hours. Timing distinguishes the other effects of diabetic pregnancy. Hyperglycemia during organogenesis in the first trimester causes structural malformations such as neural tube defects, conotruncal heart defects, and caudal regression, while hyperglycemia in the second and third trimesters causes macrosomia. Maternal vascular disease can instead reduce placental perfusion and cause growth restriction.

blocks.predict: A mother has high plasma insulin but normal glucose because of insulin resistance. Will her fetus be hyperinsulinemic?
blocks.explain: No. Maternal insulin does not cross the placenta, and fetal beta cells respond only to fetal glucose, which follows maternal glucose. Normal maternal glucose means normal fetal insulin.

sections.title: Zinc deficiency and vitamin A excess in sexual and embryonic development

blocks.text: Zinc is a cofactor for hundreds of enzymes, including DNA and RNA polymerases, alkaline phosphatase, carbonic anhydrase, and superoxide dismutase, and it forms the zinc finger DNA-binding domains of many transcription factors. Each nuclear steroid receptor, including the androgen and estrogen receptors, binds DNA through two zinc fingers. Because zinc is needed for cell division, protein synthesis, and hormone signaling, deficiency hits tissues that grow fast or depend on steroid action.

Zinc deficiency causes hypogonadism with low testosterone, impaired spermatogenesis, and delayed sexual maturation, together with growth failure. The classic descriptions came from adolescent boys in the Middle East whose diets were high in phytate, which binds zinc and blocks its absorption. Zinc is required for Leydig cell steroidogenesis and for the germinal epithelium, and the testis and prostate hold some of the highest zinc concentrations in the body. Other features follow from the same roles: poor wound healing, hypogeusia (reduced taste), alopecia, impaired cell-mediated immunity, diarrhea, and a periorificial and acral dermatitis. The inherited form, acrodermatitis enteropathica, is an autosomal recessive defect in the intestinal zinc transporter ZIP4 (SLC39A4). Acquired causes include malabsorption, chronic diarrhea, alcoholism, and cirrhosis.

Vitamin A is the opposite problem: harm from excess. Retinol is oxidized to retinal and then, irreversibly, to retinoic acid, the form that acts as a morphogen. All-trans retinoic acid binds the retinoic acid receptor (RAR), which pairs with the retinoid X receptor (RXR) on retinoic acid response elements and controls genes such as the Hox genes that specify position along the body axis. Embryos keep retinoic acid in precise gradients by making it in some tissues and degrading it with CYP26 in others. Excess preformed vitamin A or a retinoid drug such as isotretinoin (13-cis retinoic acid) floods those gradients during organogenesis, roughly weeks 3 to 8, and misdirects the hindbrain and the cranial neural crest cells that migrate into the pharyngeal arches and the cardiac outflow tract.

Overactivation of RAR/RXR and Hox signaling

Hypogonadism, low sperm count, delayed puberty

Isotretinoin or high-dose preformed vitamin A in early pregnancy
blocks.caption: Zinc deficiency removes function; retinoid excess adds signaling at the wrong time and place.

blocks.text: Retinoid embryopathy therefore has a recognizable pattern. Craniofacial defects include small, absent, or low-set ears, micrognathia, and cleft palate. Cardiac defects are conotruncal, such as tetralogy of Fallot, transposition of the great arteries, and interrupted aortic arch. Thymic hypoplasia reflects the third pharyngeal pouch, and CNS defects include hydrocephalus, microcephaly, and cerebellar malformation. Beta-carotene does not cause this, because its cleavage to retinal is regulated by vitamin A status.

sections.title: Low energy availability, leptin, and hypothalamic amenorrhea

blocks.text: Reproduction is energetically expensive, and the hypothalamus permits it only when fuel is sufficient. Energy availability is dietary intake minus exercise energy expenditure, the energy left over for every other body function. When it falls too low, whether from intense training, restricted eating, an eating disorder, or very low body fat, the reproductive axis is switched off before other systems are threatened.

Leptin is the main signal. Adipocytes secrete it in proportion to fat mass, and it also drops quickly with an acute energy deficit. GnRH neurons lack leptin receptors, so leptin acts on upstream hypothalamic neurons, largely in the arcuate nucleus, that in turn regulate the kisspeptin neurons driving GnRH release. Low leptin, together with high ghrelin, raised cortisol (CRH inhibits GnRH), low insulin and IGF-1, and low T3, slows GnRH pulse frequency and amplitude. People with congenital leptin deficiency have hypogonadotropic hypogonadism that leptin replacement reverses, which shows the signal is necessary.

blocks.title: Low energy availability to bone loss
steps: Energy intake falls below expenditure
Leptin falls; cortisol rises; insulin and IGF-1 fall
Kisspeptin drive drops; GnRH pulses slow
LH and FSH pulses fade; no dominant follicle
Low estradiol, anovulation, amenorrhea
Bone resorption rises and formation falls
Low bone density and stress fractures
blocks.caption: The reproductive axis shuts down to save energy, and the bone loss is the cost of low estrogen.

blocks.text: With slow GnRH pulses, LH pulses are too infrequent to support follicle growth, so no dominant follicle forms, estradiol stays low, and ovulation and menses stop. This is functional hypothalamic amenorrhea: a hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with low or inappropriately normal LH and FSH, low estradiol, and normal prolactin. The endometrium is thin, so a progestin challenge produces little or no withdrawal bleeding. Men show the same suppression as low testosterone.

Estrogen normally restrains bone resorption. It lowers osteoblast and stromal cell production of RANKL, raises osteoprotegerin, and shortens osteoclast lifespan. Without it, resorption rises, and low IGF-1 and insulin reduce bone formation at the same time, so bone balance turns negative from both sides. In adolescents this also prevents reaching peak bone mass, a deficit that may not fully recover. The combination of low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction, and low bone density is the female athlete triad, now viewed as part of relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S).

blocks.title: Labs that place amenorrhea in the axis

sections.title: Cholesterol supply and the StAR rate-limiting step in gonadal steroidogenesis

blocks.text: Steroid-producing cells store very little hormone, so output depends on how fast cholesterol reaches the first enzyme. Gonads and placenta can make cholesterol from acetyl-CoA through HMG-CoA reductase, but in humans most of their substrate comes from circulating LDL. LDL binds the LDL receptor through apolipoprotein B-100, enters by clathrin-mediated endocytosis, and is delivered to lysosomes, where acid lipase frees cholesterol. HDL cholesterol taken up through scavenger receptor B1 contributes a smaller share. Cholesterol not used at once is stored as cholesteryl ester in lipid droplets and released by a hormone-sensitive cholesteryl ester hydrolase.

blocks.title: LDL cholesterol to pregnenolone in a Leydig or theca cell
steps: LH binds its Gs-coupled receptor; cAMP and PKA rise
LDL receptors import LDL; lysosomes free cholesterol
Stored cholesteryl esters are hydrolyzed
Cholesterol reaches the outer mitochondrial membrane
StAR moves it to the inner membrane (rate-limiting)
CYP11A1 cleaves the side chain to pregnenolone
blocks.caption: LH speeds both cholesterol supply and its delivery into mitochondria.

blocks.text: The side-chain cleavage enzyme CYP11A1 sits on the inner mitochondrial membrane, but cholesterol is poorly soluble and moves slowly across the aqueous space between the membranes. StAR moves it from the outer to the inner membrane, and this transfer, not the enzyme reaction, sets the overall rate. LH, acting through cAMP and protein kinase A, increases StAR within minutes by phosphorylating it and by inducing new StAR synthesis, which is why the acute steroid response depends on ongoing protein synthesis. Over longer periods LH also raises LDL receptor and CYP11A1 expression.

blocks.title: Where steroidogenic cells get cholesterol
rows: LDL plus de novo synthesis; LH raises uptake
LDL from its blood supply; LH-driven
Little LDL (avascular, inside the basement membrane)
Mainly LDL, available once vessels invade
Progesterone; estrogens only from fetal (and maternal) DHEA-S
blocks.caption: Access to blood-borne LDL explains why granulosa cells make large amounts of progesterone only after luteinization.

blocks.text: The placenta is an incomplete steroid organ. It takes up maternal LDL and converts cholesterol to pregnenolone and progesterone, using the related protein MLN64 rather than StAR, but lacks 17-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP17). It cannot make androgens and must use DHEA-S from the fetal adrenal, 16-hydroxylated in the fetal liver, to make estriol, so maternal estriol reflects the fetal adrenal and liver as well as the placenta.

Loss of StAR causes congenital lipoid adrenal hyperplasia. Cholesterol accumulates in lipid droplets and damages adrenal and gonadal cells, so almost no steroids are made: adrenal insufficiency in all patients and female external genitalia in 46,XY individuals. Loss of LDL receptors in familial hypercholesterolemia, by contrast, largely spares steroid output because de novo synthesis and HDL uptake compensate.

blocks.predict: Why does StAR deficiency nearly abolish steroid synthesis while LDL receptor deficiency barely affects it?
blocks.explain: StAR controls the single route of cholesterol into the inner mitochondrial membrane, the only place CYP11A1 can act. LDL receptors are one of several supply routes; de novo synthesis and HDL can replace them.

integration.text: Each nutrient in this chapter acts through a mechanism taught in another discipline. Folate and iron are biochemistry and hematology applied to pregnancy. Folate and retinoic acid act at defined windows of embryology, neurulation in weeks 3 and 4 and neural crest migration during organogenesis, so the defects they cause are predictable from timing. Glucose transfer and fetal insulin connect placental physiology to endocrine pathology, and secretory IgA in milk links lactation to mucosal immunology.

Energy and cholesterol show how supply controls hormone output. The hypothalamus reads leptin and other metabolic signals before allowing GnRH pulses, and steroidogenic cells depend on StAR to move cholesterol where CYP11A1 can act. Limits apply: neural tube defects are multifactorial and not all are folate related, ferritin can be falsely normal with inflammation, and reference ranges for hemoglobin, ferritin, and milk composition differ among sources, so values here are approximate.

summary: Folate, reduced by DHFR to THF, supplies the one-carbon unit for dTMP and carbons 2 and 8 of purines; thymidylate synthase oxidizes folate to DHF each time it acts.
Thymidylate shortage causes uracil misincorporation and strand breaks in dividing cells, and the neural tube must close by about day 28, so folate must be adequate at conception.
Pregnancy needs about 1 g of extra iron; plasma volume rises about 40 to 50% and red cell mass about 20 to 30%, causing dilutional anemia.
Ferritin separates iron deficiency (low) from dilution (normal); TIBC rises in all pregnancies, and MCV falls only after stores are gone.
Lactose synthase is galactosyltransferase redirected by alpha-lactalbumin; lactose is the osmole that sets milk volume.
Human milk is high in lactose, low in protein, whey dominant, and rich in secretory IgA, lactoferrin, and lysozyme, but low in vitamins D and K.
Glucose crosses the placenta by GLUT1 and insulin does not, so maternal hyperglycemia causes fetal hyperinsulinemia, macrosomia, polycythemia, delayed surfactant, and neonatal hypoglycemia.
Zinc deficiency causes hypogonadism and delayed puberty; excess retinoids disrupt RAR and Hox signaling and cranial neural crest, causing craniofacial, conotruncal, thymic, and CNS defects.
Low energy availability and low leptin slow GnRH pulses, producing hypothalamic amenorrhea with low estrogen and bone loss.
Gonads and placenta take cholesterol mainly from LDL; StAR transfer into the inner mitochondrial membrane is the rate-limiting step, and LH accelerates it through cAMP.

verify: Cranial and caudal neuropore closure days (about 25 and 27 to 28) vary by one or two days among embryology texts; confirm the value NABNE uses.
Folic acid supplement doses (about 0.4 mg daily, higher after a prior affected pregnancy) are management content omitted from Part I teaching here; confirm whether NABNE Part I tests them.
Iron budget components (about 450 to 500 mg red cell mass, 300 mg fetus and placenta, 200 mg basal losses) and red cell mass expansion (quoted 20 to 35%) vary among obstetric and physiology sources.

Hemoglobin cutoffs for anemia in pregnancy (commonly below 11 g/dL in the first and third trimesters and 10.5 g/dL in the second) and the ferritin cutoff for iron deficiency (30 ng/mL versus 15 ng/mL) differ between guidelines.
Human milk composition figures (lactose about 7 g/dL, protein about 0.9 to 1.2 g/dL, whey to casein about 60:40) change with stage of lactation and vary by source.
Fetal to maternal glucose ratio (about 70 to 80%) and the birth weight threshold for macrosomia (4,000 g or 4,500 g) vary by source.
The precise mechanism linking zinc deficiency to impaired Leydig cell steroidogenesis is incompletely defined; the chapter states the established association and the zinc finger and enzyme roles.
The vitamin A intake above which teratogenic risk rises (often quoted near 10,000 IU daily of preformed vitamin A) is debated; confirm whether NABNE expects a number.
The energy availability threshold for suppression of LH pulsatility (about 30 kcal per kg fat-free mass per day) comes from research studies and may not be tested.
Placental use of MLN64 (STARD3) in place of StAR is described in Boron and Boulpaep and specialty reviews; confirm NABNE expects this level of detail.
A schematic of the folate cycle and of the steroidogenic cell (LDL receptor, lysosome, StAR, CYP11A1) would help; requested diagram names: folate-cycle and steroidogenic-cell.
